opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think people sometimes imagine that being part of a large group means every decision gets handed down from above, and that hasn't really been my experience. On a question like whether to build our own robot body, the discussion was very much driven by the team itself, by what we think the technology actually needs.

What Ant brings is less about telling us what to do and more about giving us room to think long-term. Embodied intelligence isn't something you solve in one or two product cycles. If you're a small startup, you're under huge pressure to show a demo or ship something quickly, and that can push you toward decisions that look good in the short run but don't necessarily lead you to a real breakthrough. Having the backing of a larger organization means we can afford to ask, "What is the right path?" rather than "What can we show next quarter?"

On the body question specifically, my own view is that the hardware and the intelligence can't be fully separated. If you only work on models and rely entirely on someone else's platform, you're always constrained by choices you didn't make: the sensors, the degrees of freedom, how data gets collected. At the same time, building hardware from scratch is extremely expensive and slow, and it's not our core strength yet. So it's a real trade-off, and we discussed it openly. Ant's role in that conversation was more like a partner asking hard questions: Where's your differentiation? What's the long-term value? Is this the best use of resources? Those are fair questions, and they made our thinking sharper.

So I'd describe it as support with accountability. They trust the team to make the technical judgments, but they also expect us to explain clearly why a direction makes sense. For a research-driven group like ours, I think that's actually a pretty healthy relationship.

r001.rationale: The response says Ant trusts the team to make technical judgments, but does not attribute that trust to Lingbo being closer to the robotics industry.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, Ant has been quite hands-off on those decisions. When we set up Lingbo, the understanding from the beginning was that this is a long-term bet, and long-term bets don't work if the parent company is micromanaging each technical choice. So on the question of whether to build the body ourselves, that was really a decision made inside the team, based on what we believed was necessary for the research.

The way I think about it is: Ant provides the resources and the patience. They care about the direction, and we have regular conversations about where embodied intelligence is going and why it matters strategically. But they don't tell us "build hardware" or "don't build hardware." That would be a strange thing for them to decide, because frankly the people closest to the problem are the ones who understand the tradeoffs.

And the tradeoffs here are real. If you only do software and buy bodies from others, you're constrained by whatever the hardware vendor optimized for, and the data you collect is shaped by that body. If you build your own, you control the whole loop, but you take on enormous cost and complexity, and hardware moves slowly compared to models. We spent a lot of time debating this internally, and the conclusion was that we needed enough control over the body to run the experiments we wanted, without turning into a hardware company. That is a nuanced position, and I don't think a parent company could have reached it from the outside.

What Ant does bring, beyond funding, is a certain kind of grounding. They ask good questions about where this eventually becomes useful, and that keeps us honest. But the day-to-day judgment calls are ours, and I think that's the right structure.

r001.rationale: The response says Lingbo’s team is closest to the problem and understands the technical tradeoffs, but it does not attribute Ant’s trust to Lingbo being closer to the robotics industry.

Does building it ourselves help us develop and validate the technology, or would working with a hardware partner be more effective? That’s how I’d frame the decision. I wouldn’t characterize Ant’s involvement more specifically without knowing the internal discussions.
